title: Buried with Christ in Baptism
english: …has made [a declaration of the whole]. So the one who names Christ will not leave the Father or the Spirit unremembered. But since Jesus, having become man, endured death for the life of all, the blessed Paul had to go on to what was most needful for the sacred teaching at hand, for he had to name the one who suffered. That is why he says, “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Romans 6:3).

For having first given, as it were, the good pledge of an upright conscience toward Christ (1 Peter 3:21), and having accepted by faith that he died for us, was buried, and came to life again, we have received the forgiveness of sins through holy baptism. We undergo the deadening of sin, and as it were die together with him who died for us, by putting to death our members that are on the earth (Colossians 3:5). For Christ “died to sin once for all, but the life he lives, he lives to God” (Romans 6:10). We undergo a death equal to his and are all but buried with him, carrying about his dying in our own bodies (2 Corinthians 4:10); and we were buried with Christ (Romans 6:4). What we gain from this he will make clear himself, saying, “so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). For since we have been buried with him, we must also rise with him spiritually. And if being buried with Christ is having died to sin, then surely it is clear that rising with him can rightly be understood as nothing other than living in righteousness.

He affirms, indeed, that Christ was raised through the glory of the Father, not as though Christ lacked strength, for he himself is the Lord of hosts (Psalm 24:10), but because it is the custom of Christ himself and of his own to ascribe what is beyond human nature to the glory of the supreme nature. So even if God the Father is said to accomplish something, he does not shut the Son out of his activity over all things. For if all things came into being through him (John 1:3), how could anyone doubt that he worked through the Son the resurrection of that holy body as well? Indeed the Son, showing himself active in this, said to the Jews, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). See, then, how he promises to raise his own temple himself, although God the Father is said to have raised it. For since he is himself the life-giving power of God the Father, he gave life to his own temple.

“For if we have been united with the likeness of his death,” and so on (Romans 6:5). The inspired Paul says that those who have been buried with Christ ought also to expect to rise with him. The word “united” would suggest, in a spiritual sense, something like “conformed” and “of the same form.” But this point must be examined closely. Emmanuel laid down his own life for us (1 John 3:16) and died according to the flesh. In what way, then, have we who are baptized been buried with him? Was it by enduring with him the death of the flesh? Not at all. How, then, have we been united with the likeness of his death? Come, then, let us say it. He died…
translator_notes: Opens with ἐποιήσατο, the main verb of the sentence that ends u02-rem-close (κἂν εἰ ἕν τις ὀνομάσῃ, δυνάμει θεωρημάτων τὴν τοῦ παντὸς δήλωσιν). The bracketed words '[a declaration of the whole]' repeat that object only so the fragment reads; they add nothing new.
Ends mid-sentence at ἀπέθανε; u03-rem-early continues μὲν γὰρ κατὰ σάρκα Χριστός. The closing ellipsis marks the break.

οὐκ ἐξ οἰκείου μὲν τῆς ἐφ' ἅπασιν ἐνεργείας αὐτοῦ τὸν Υἱόν: the clause has no verb and looks damaged in the copy-text (most likely a misreading of οὐκ ἐξοικίζει, 'does not shut out'). Rendered by that reading and the evident sense: the Father does not shut the Son out of his activity over all things.
ὅτι καὶ ἀπέθανεν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν καὶ ἐτάφη καὶ ἀνεβίω: possible echo of the creed-like 1 Corinthians 15:3-4, but the wording differs (ἀνεβίω, not ἐγήγερται); left uncited as uncertain.
σύμφυτοι (literally 'grown together, planted together') is rendered 'united' to match the lemma; Cyril himself explains it as σύμμορφοι and ταυτοειδεῖς.
νοητῶς rendered 'spiritually' (in the inward, understood sense, not bodily).
ὁ τῶν δυνάμεων Κύριος rendered 'the Lord of hosts', the usual English for this LXX title.
PG column number 190 and stray quotation marks inside the Scripture quotations in the copy-text are dropped from the reading text.
